syllabus.clause: B+-trees, LSM-trees and their filters as the index layer

at.step: A lookup for a key that is not there should touch no data block at all. Yet one filter block alone can be over a thousand times the size of the data block it protects. Predict: what does the engine do with a filter bigger than the thing it is supposed to protect, and what does that remind you of?

The textbook contract, and the system's addition, side by side: the Chapter 5 B+-tree exactly as drawn there, key only, on the left; a storage engine's leaf entry on the right, a second value riding beside the key.

PostgreSQL's requirement that every btree key be unique is met by treating the heap tuple identifier as a tiebreaker attribute: logical duplicates of the same key are sorted in heap TID order, so no two entries are ever truly identical.

Measured: five order rows for the same customer become five leaf entries. The key repeats five times, but each entry's tuple identifier is different, so every entry is unique and the tree's ordering still holds.

Predict: a leaf page fills up with entries that all share one key and must split. Does the split put half the duplicates on each side of the new boundary, the way a split of ordinary, distinct keys would?
Measured on the shop's five duplicate rows at a small leaf capacity: the left page keeps every slot it had, full; the right page holds only the one row the split pushed out, almost empty.
The second structure, the same way: the Chapter 5 LSM tree exactly as drawn there on the left; RocksDB's stored key on the right, a sequence number now riding beside the user key.
RocksDB's comparator orders by user key ascending, then by sequence number descending: among entries for the same key, the newest write sorts first, drawn as a stack with the newest version on top.

Measured: one key is written three times and then deleted. A snapshot taken right after the second write still reads the second write's value, untouched by everything that came later; a reader with no snapshot constraint sees the delete, ahead of every earlier version.

Because the newest version already sorts first, a snapshot read is one seek to the first version at or before the snapshot, never a scan of every version a key ever had. The same ordering is what a later topic's merging iterator reads when it walks several files at once.

The filter problem, stated in full: one index or filter block is commonly far larger than a single data block, so when it is not cached it competes with the very data blocks it exists to protect, and kicks them out of the cache.

The fix: the filter is split into small partitions, with a tiny top-level index over them, itself only a sliver of the filter's own size, loaded once; a lookup loads only the one partition it actually needs, on demand.

Predict, then measured: four point lookups, counted in block reads. A hit costs the same whether or not a filter exists, since the data still has to be fetched. A miss with no filter wastes exactly one data read. A miss against a whole filter already in the cache costs nothing extra. A miss whose one needed filter partition is not cached costs one more read: exactly as much as having no filter at all.

The RocksDB internal-key ordering example is built from the comparator's own documented rule (user key ascending, sequence descending) rather than from reading an actual on-disk SST file, a deliberate scope choice stated in OUTLINE.md: the topic verifies the stated rule by simulation, not by inspecting real bytes, which the builder's environment has no running RocksDB instance to produce.
